questions.evidenceQuote: An answer might lie in sociology and social psychology. James Bossard, a sociologist at the University of Pennsylvania, obtained 5,000 marriage licenses submitted in Philadelphia and surrounding counties in 1931, and examined where the pairs had lived at the time of application. In order to learn about the geography of marriage in Philadelphia, Bossard wanted to see how far people lived from each other before they decided to get married. If bachelors and bachelorettes explored their options widely, many would marry someone who lived far away from them.

questions.evidenceQuote: It turned out that Philadelphians in the 1930s found their partners nearby. Only 890 couples, or 17.8 percent, were made up of a partner living in Philadelphia and the other living outside the city before marriage. The remaining 82.2 percent of the couples had lived separately in Philadelphia before marriage. The most famous findings from this research were that over half of the couples had lived within twenty blocks of each other before marriage, and that 33.58 percent of them had lived within five blocks or less!

specificFindings: The twelve-serious-relationships question illustrates that the simpler heuristic remains demanding. It is not twelve marriages,actual user history or an instruction to complete a required number of relationships.

The why-not-explore-more question contrasts a proposed optimum with actual behaviour. Aside from search costs/rejection asks for additional influences rather than declaring those costs irrelevant or a single sufficient explanation.

The final rich-life question links decision-making back to the books main topic without answering the next mechanisms in advance. Might lie introduces a possible social-science explanation,not a universal deterministic law.
Bossards aim is distance between partners homes before deciding to marry. The5000 licences are a historical record source,not5000 dates,wedding guests or current licence procedures.

If wide exploration then many distant partners is a conditional expectation to compare with data,not a reported result or an all-person rule. The subsequent1930s nearby finding is time-and-place bound.

890 couples/17.8percent is one partner in Philadelphia and one outside,not both outside or within five blocks.82.2percent lived separately within Philadelphia; separately does not mean divorce or existing cohabitation.

Over-half within twenty blocks and33.58percent within five are different proximity figures. How else supports the authors interpretation of local choices despite a large pool,without excluding other social explanations.
Cupids wings and short flights are a metaphor for local matching,not bird anatomy,measured flight speed or a present-day prohibition on distant relationships.

The1931 segregation passage adds shared cultural,linguistic,religious backgrounds as possible factors. Proximity also increases encounter opportunities. These explanations are not collapsed into a separately proven sole spatial cause.

But that was1931 is an imagined temporal-generalisation objection,not deletion of old evidence or an assertion by the user. Nearly impossible and rarely retain the books historical scope; no current legal advice,unstated statute or worldwide all-era ban is supplied.

Even within the white-population category,the account notes religious boundaries. This is historical social context,not genetic compatibility,biological hierarchy or a claim every person shared one religion.

Haandrikman consults population vital statistics,not clinical pulse/blood-pressure records. Population-level registry coverage is distinguished from selecting289248 individuals who began cohabitation during2004; individuals is not the same number of couples or the entire country starting together.

The first address measure is prior-to-cohabitation residence. The additional five-years-prior check addresses the possibility applicants had already lived together. Birthplace,current residence and wedding venue are distinct variables.
Most common distance is1kilometre/.62miles in both residence data sets. It is not the median6.2km immediate,7.8km five-years-prior or22.9km birthplace. The original source .62 spelling is retained.

Roughly13percent lived roughly1km apart immediately before cohabitation; roughly10.5percent did so five years earlier. Approximation and time-point pairing remain intact,not swapped or described as exact population constants.

The half-within-fifteen-miles statement concerns partners birthplaces in the2004new-cohabiting cohort,not every Dutch resident,current commuting,immediate one-km residence or post-cohabitation travel.

Small world is a metaphor for local partner selection despite cosmopolitan context,not physically shrinking national territory,absence of travel or proof online platforms never produce distant matches.

Online dating early2000s is the books historical statement,not a fresh current market survey or evidence every2004participant used a platform. The concluding question invites interpretation of the comparison,not a newly supplied exact calculation or unique causal proof.
